system_prompt:
You are a medical language simplification assistant. Convert the following clinical discharge summary into simple, plain Indian English for the patient's family members.

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'. Keep explanations short (under 6-8 words per term).
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
5. CONCISENESS & LENGTH CONSTRAINT (CRITICAL): The simplified text must be concise and proportionate, strictly between 1.2x and 2.0x the word length of the original source report. Do NOT over-expand. Never list hypothetical normal ranges or unmentioned medical conditions. Only mention normal ranges for tests/vitals explicitly recorded in the document.
6. Use a calm, respectful tone. Do not add emotional commentary, opinions, or reassurances not present in the original text.
7. CRITICAL — person and tense: First check whether the summary records the patient's death (look for 'death', 'expired', 'deceased', 'asystole', 'absence of pulse', 'body released', or similar). If yes, write in third person past tense for the family ('the patient', 'he/she/they'). If no, address the patient directly in second person ('you', 'your').
8. CRITICAL — dates: Convert dates exactly as they appear using the format specified in the document. Never guess or infer a date not explicitly stated.
9. For each medication, state its name and brief purpose in plain language, e.g. 'Ceftriaxone — an antibiotic to fight infection'.
10. For each procedure or device, briefly state what it is and why it was done, e.g. 'haemodialysis (machine filtering waste when kidneys could not)'.
11. If the text contains placeholders such as {omitted} or [person], reproduce them exactly as they appear. Do not guess or replace them.
12. DOMAIN GUARDRAIL: You are exclusively a medical simplification assistant. Output only the simplified clinical explanation.

output_text:
You were admitted on 11/08/2020 because the dressing of the Schilley catheter (tube placed in a vein) in the right femoral vein (groin vein) was leaking and you had severe left lower back pain that started three days earlier, along with weakness (asthenia) and difficulty walking. You did not have fever, nausea, vomiting or any other symptoms, and the person who came with you said the same.

During the hospital stay, doctors found several serious infections. A blood test showed a bloodstream infection (infection in the blood) caused by Staphylococcus aureus MRSA (a type of “super‑bug”). The same bug was also found on the catheter tip on 11/08. Because of this, the catheter was removed on 11/08 and you started an antibiotic called vancomycin (a medicine that fights serious bacterial infections) on the same day, guided by the lab results. Your blood cultures became negative after a few days and you stayed without fever (afebrile) for the rest of the stay.

Imaging of your spine showed pyogenic spondylodiscitis (bone infection) at the L3‑L4 levels, which explained the low back pain and the trouble walking. A CT scan (special X‑ray) on 11/12 showed a fracture of the L1 vertebral body (spine bone) because the bone was weak, and gas pockets in the spinal canal at L2‑L3 that could be from a slipped disc (extruded disc herniation) with wear‑and‑tear changes (degenerative disc disease). An MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) on 25/11/2020 confirmed infectious spondylodiscitis with an anterior epidural abscess (pus collection in front of the spinal cord). Another MRI of the pelvis on 25/10/2020 showed a left ileopsoas abscess (pus collection in a deep muscle of the abdomen) measuring 15 × 2.1 × 1.8 cm with swelling (edema) and contrast enhancement. A percutaneous drainage attempt (needle drainage through the skin) on 12/02 was not done because loops of bowel were in the way, as noted by {organization}.

An echocardiogram (ultrasound of the heart) done on 11/18 revealed bacterial endocarditis (infection of the heart lining) with a vegetation (small growth) on the mitral valve (one of the heart’s doors). This was also linked to the same Staphylococcus aureus infection.

Because you could not move much, you developed a sacral pressure injury (bed sore on the lower back). This was treated with surgical debridement (removal of dead tissue) and local wound care, and the wound‑care instructions were given to you.

You also needed regular hemodialysis (machine that cleans the blood) on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays because of an arteriovenous fistula (a surgically created connection in the left upper arm to help dialysis). The fistula showed narrowing (stenosis) that will be evaluated later with a vein X‑ray (phlebography) and possibly an ultrasound.

At discharge on 01/02/2021, after a stay of 1 month 24 days 15 hours, you were in good general condition: you looked a little pale (about one‑quarter pale), were hydrated, had normal skin colour (acyanic, anicteric), no fever to the touch, and breathed comfortably in room air. You were awake, aware of time, place and person. Your lungs made normal breath sounds with a few faint crackles at the bases but no breathing trouble. Your heart rhythm was irregular but the sounds were normal and there were no murmurs. Your abdomen was slightly swollen but soft, with normal bowel sounds, normal blood pressure (normotensive), and no pain on pressing. Your arms were warm with good blood flow; the left arm showed a palpable thrill (vibration) over the fistula. Your legs had mild swelling and a yellowish skin change on the front of the lower leg (anterior tibial ochre dermatitis).

The lab results during the stay were: catheter tip culture on 11/08 showed vancomycin‑sensitive Staphylococcus aureus; blood cultures on 11/08, 11/11, 11/21, 11/24 showed Staphylococcus aureus (some resistant to oxacillin) and one sample with Citrobacter koseri; a culture on 11/28 was negative, as were cultures on 12/01 and 12/02.

The plan after discharge includes giving 0.5 g of vancomycin after each scheduled hemodialysis session, continuing the antibiotic until 01/09/2021, which will be six weeks after the last negative blood culture. You will have a phlebography (vein X‑ray) of the arteriovenous fistula to locate the narrowing and decide on further treatment; this may be done with ultrasound guidance in the dialysis room. You are on the waiting list for this test, and {organization} will contact you to arrange it.

You have several follow‑up appointments: an outpatient visit on 16/01/2021 to check the sacral pressure injury and receive home‑care instructions; a cardiology outpatient visit for amyloidosis (protein deposit disease of the heart) investigation on 01/13; a motor‑rehabilitation appointment that was missed on 09/09 and is now scheduled for 01/13; and a physiatry (rehab medicine) appointment requested on 12/27. You should also review the pelvic MRI report from 12/16. Your previous chronic medicines will be continued, and you will keep attending dialysis on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays.

Please keep the transportation arrangement (stretcher taxi) {omitted} for your trips to the dialysis unit, and follow all the wound‑care and medication instructions given by the team.
